summary.text: 鸡 is the simplified form used for “chicken.” Its traditional counterpart 雞 is understood as an early bird picture, later written in compound forms with a bird element and 奚 as a sound element. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so the picture’s original referent is uncertain.

formation.text: The traditional graph 雞 is phonosemantic in later forms: 隹 or 鳥 contributes the bird category, and 奚 supplies a sound cue. Early forms are also interpreted as a whole chicken picture. The evidence does not give a fully dated sequence from picture to compound. The modern shape 鸡 does not establish a historical 又 + 鸟 construction.

components.text: Early forms of 雞 are interpreted as a whole picture of a chicken, with the crest and open beak emphasized. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so the picture’s original referent is uncertain.

In 雞, 奚 supplies sound, not its separate lexical meaning. The Middle Chinese readings share a rhyme but differ in initial; the Old Chinese comparison is approximate and comes from a local cross-check.

sound_limitation.text: The exact Old Chinese forms in the local cross-check were not verified at the dataset publisher. The historical dictionary explicitly assigns 奚 a sound role in 雞.

sound.text: Modern Mandarin readings xī and jī differ. This modern pair alone does not establish the historical sound relation.
The supplied Middle Chinese forms share a rhyme but differ in initial.

components.text: 隹 contributes the bird category in Qin and later forms of 雞. Some Warring States Qi and Chu forms instead use 鳥; the evidence does not establish a single sequence between these bird elements.

鳮 is recorded as a simplified-style variant associated with 雞 and appears as 鳮（雞） in the 1956 simplification scheme. The precise graphic route to 鸡 is not documented; 又 has no supported historical role in 鸡.

history.text: A selected oracle-script image is a modern redraw of a form interpreted as a chicken picture, not an ancient inscription. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name. One account says 奚 was later added as a sound marker because the picture could be confused with other birds, but the sequence is not fully dated.

The bird element varies across forms: some Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin and later forms use 隹. 鷄 is described as a Zhou-script form written with 鳥 and is treated as a graphic variant of 雞; the evidence does not establish a single linear path between them.
The 1956 simplification scheme lists 鳮（雞） and simplifies 鳥 as 鸟. It does not document the precise graphic route to 鸡 or support analyzing 鸡 as a historical 又 + 鸟 compound.

uncertainties.text: Early 雞 is interpreted as a chicken picture, but the earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name. The picture’s original referent and earliest lexical meaning, and the timing of any transition to a compound, remain uncertain.
The bird element appears as both 鳥 and 隹 in different script traditions and periods. The evidence does not establish a complete sequence or show that 鳥 was only a later replacement.
The simplification evidence associates 鳮 with 雞 and lists 鳮（雞）, but does not document the precise graphic steps to standardized 鸡.

senses.text: A Qin bamboo-slip passage is reported to use 雞 for chicken. The oracle-bone place-name use does not show whether this was the graph’s earliest animal meaning.

senses.period: oracle-bone script tradition; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: An oracle-bone use of 雞 is reported as a place name. This shows a use of the graph but does not establish the place-name’s referent or the graph’s original lexical meaning.

senses.gloss: 谿, valley or stream, written with 雞
senses.period: Mawangdui manuscript witness; exact borrowing date unresolved
senses.text: In a Mawangdui text, 雞 is reported as a phonetic loan for 谿, “valley” or “stream”; another manuscript copy has 溪. The written sign was reused for a different word, apparently on the basis of sound similarity, rather than “chicken” developing into “valley.” The reported account supplies no contemporary pronunciations to demonstrate the sound match.
The common current meaning is chicken.

limitations.text: The reported oracle-bone place-name use and Qin-slip animal use do not establish a direct semantic transition between them or identify the picture’s earliest lexical value.
The reported Mawangdui loan lacks contemporary pronunciations and a demonstrated sound rationale; its motivation and timing remain unresolved.

overview.text: 鸡 means “chicken.” Its traditional graph 雞 is interpreted as an early chicken picture, with later forms analyzed as a compound containing a bird element and sound-bearing 奚. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so the picture’s original referent is uncertain.

Another 奚 kind of bird 隹
Originally was a pictograph of a chicken. Later changed to a phonosemantic compound of 奚 and 隹 (bird).
知時畜也。从隹奚聲。

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *keː): phonetic 奚 (OC *ɡeː) + semantic 隹 (“short-tailed bird”).
Onomatopoeic (Schuessler, 2007). Compare Proto-Vietic *r-kaa (> Vietnamese gà), Proto-Tai *kajᴮ (“chicken”), Proto-Hmong-Mien *Kəi.
* (to fire): From 無情雞 /无情鸡 (mou⁴ cing⁴ gai¹, “pink slip”).

evidence.source: 中央研究院漢字構形資料庫（Character Structure Database）
evidence.text: The database describes the bronze form of 雞 as a whole-figure pictograph of a chicken that later developed into a phonosemantic form with 隹 as semantic element and 奚 as phonetic element. It identifies a bronze specimen as 集成05802. This supports a development from pictorial graph to compound, but the page gives no date for that individual specimen.
evidence.title: 漢字「雞」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義通解; 早期用例
evidence.text: The database analyzes early oracle forms as chicken pictures, often emphasizing the comb and open beak; it says 奚 was later added as a phonetic marker because the picture could be confused with other birds. It reports an oracle-bone use as a place name in 《合集》37363 and cites Qin bamboo slips from the Shuihudi annals (簡45), “十二月甲午雞鳴時，喜產,” as a use referring to chickens. It separately reports Chicken as the ordinary sense in Warring States/Qin slips and a Mawangdui silk text. In Mawangdui 《老子乙本》 line 65, 雞 is used as a phonetic loan for 谿 “valley/stream,” with the A copy reading 溪 and the Fu Yi text 谿. The page distinguishes these written uses rather than presenting a gloss list as a chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 《說文》; 字形分析; 音韻資料
evidence.text: The page transmits the Eastern Han Shuowen account: “雞，知時畜也。从隹，奚聲。鷄，籒文雞，从鳥。” Its account says Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin forms and later use 隹, citing Ji Xusheng. This variation complicates a simple story that 鳥 was only a later substitute for 隹. It gives Guangyun fanqie 古奚 and Middle Chinese categories 見母, 平聲, 齊韻, 開口四等.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, digital text of 說文解字 and 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.field: 卷四 隹部; 鷄 entry
evidence.text: The page gives the Shuowen definition “知時畜也。从隹奚聲,” the fanqie 古兮切, and “鷄，籒文雞从鳥.” This is a historical dictionary account, not independent paleographic confirmation of the origin. The page itself supplies no dated early attestation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「雞」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 奚甲骨部件分析; 形義通解
evidence.text: The database analyzes 奚 in oracle script as hand/爪 plus a bound person, interpreting the graph as a person led by the hair and giving “slave/servant” as its original sense. It reports oracle uses for a place name and human sacrifice, and a bronze inscription use for a female slave. It also records that Shuowen instead glosses 奚 as 大腹 and analyzes it as 从亣、𦃟省聲; the database judges that gloss inconsistent with the early graphic form. These analyses concern 奚 in its own graph history; they do not make 奚 semantically meaningful in 雞, where Shuowen explicitly assigns it a phonetic role.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：奚

evidence.source: Local structured dataset: sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv; inspected rows 1444–1445 and 3613–3614. Verified against inspected external pages at the upstream dataset publisher could not be established.
evidence.text: Local rows give 雞 and 鷄 as Mandarin jī, Middle Chinese kej, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤe; 奚 as Mandarin xī, Middle Chinese hej, Old Chinese *[g]ˤe (with one row also giving the note “dial. for 何 *[g]ˤaj?”). In this dataset the pair shares the rhyme and differs in reconstructed initial, so their Old Chinese comparison is approximate rather than identity. These spellings are the dataset’s own Baxter–Sagart notation and must not be merged with other Old Chinese systems. Local row metadata is not treated as externally verified evidence because no official upstream HTTP page for the exact rows was inspected.
evidence.title: Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction (upstream site; exact TSV rows not verified there)

evidence.field: 雞／雞字源字形; 康熙字典; 音韻方言
evidence.text: The opened entry gives modern Mandarin IPA [tɕi˥], Cantonese gai1, and the transmitted Shuowen/Guangyun entries. It lists oracle forms, late Shang bronze examples, Chu slips, Shuowen forms, and Qin slips as separate script witnesses. Its dictionary material cites early classical chicken references including 《詩·鄭風》“女曰鷄鳴”; these establish early literary use but do not by themselves date the graph’s semantic development. It also records later senses and compounds such as insect names, fungi, and plants; these are lexical extensions or compounds, not evidence for the graph’s original formation.
evidence.title: 鸡 jī - 漢典

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, Taiwan Ministry of Education
evidence.text: The dictionary treats 鷄 as a graphic variant of 雞, citing Shuowen’s statement that it is the Zhou-script form written with 鳥, and records later dictionaries treating 鷄 and 雞 as equivalent in sound and meaning. It also records 鳮 as a variant and cites a cross-strait simplification comparison associating 鷄 with that form. This supports 鳮 as an attested simplified-style variant; the inspected page does not establish that modern simplified 鸡 arose by a single direct historical replacement of 奚 with 又.
evidence.title: [A04465-001] 鷄 (雞) - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 中华人民共和国国务院, 《汉字简化方案》 digital transcription at Wikisource
evidence.field: 国务院决议; 汉字简化第二表; 汉字偏旁简化表
evidence.text: The 1956-01-28 resolution says the first table was to be used from 1956-02-01 and lists 230 simplified characters; the second table lists 鳮（雞）. The component table lists 鸟（鳥）. This documents the officially published simplified spelling’s relation to 鳮 and the simplified bird component. It does not independently explain the pre-1956 history of 鳮, nor warrant saying that 鸡 formed historically as a semantic compound 又 + 鸟.
evidence.title: 汉字简化方案

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The database reports a Mawangdui silk manuscript use of 雞通假為谿, meaning valley/stream; it contrasts the A copy’s 溪. This is a whole-graph phonetic loan in that textual use, distinct from 奚’s role as a sound element inside the compound 雞. The page does not supply the phonetic values at the time of borrowing or establish the direction and precise date of the loan beyond the manuscript witness.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

evidence.text: The page transmits the Eastern Han Shuowen account: “雞，知時畜也。从隹，奚聲。鷄，籒文雞，从鳥。” Its account says Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin forms and later use 隹, citing Ji Xusheng. This variation complicates a simple story that 鳥 was only a later substitute for 隹. It gives Guangyun fanqie 古奚 and Middle Chinese categories 見母, 平聲, 齊韻, 開口四等.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, digital text of 說文解字 and 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.field: 卷四 隹部; 鷄 entry
evidence.text: The page gives the Shuowen definition “知時畜也。从隹奚聲,” the fanqie 古兮切, and “鷄，籒文雞从鳥.” This is a historical dictionary account, not independent paleographic confirmation of the origin. The page itself supplies no dated early attestation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「雞」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 奚甲骨部件分析; 形義通解
evidence.text: The database analyzes 奚 in oracle script as hand/爪 plus a bound person, interpreting the graph as a person led by the hair and giving “slave/servant” as its original sense. It reports oracle uses for a place name and human sacrifice, and a bronze inscription use for a female slave. It also records that Shuowen instead glosses 奚 as 大腹 and analyzes it as 从亣、𦃟省聲; the database judges that gloss inconsistent with the early graphic form. These analyses concern 奚 in its own graph history; they do not make 奚 semantically meaningful in 雞, where Shuowen explicitly assigns it a phonetic role.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：奚

evidence.source: Local structured dataset: sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv; inspected rows 1444–1445 and 3613–3614. Verified against inspected external pages at the upstream dataset publisher could not be established.
evidence.text: Local rows give 雞 and 鷄 as Mandarin jī, Middle Chinese kej, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤe; 奚 as Mandarin xī, Middle Chinese hej, Old Chinese *[g]ˤe (with one row also giving the note “dial. for 何 *[g]ˤaj?”). In this dataset the pair shares the rhyme and differs in reconstructed initial, so their Old Chinese comparison is approximate rather than identity. These spellings are the dataset’s own Baxter–Sagart notation and must not be merged with other Old Chinese systems. Local row metadata is not treated as externally verified evidence because no official upstream HTTP page for the exact rows was inspected.
evidence.title: Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction (upstream site; exact TSV rows not verified there)

evidence.field: 雞／雞字源字形; 康熙字典; 音韻方言
evidence.text: The opened entry gives modern Mandarin IPA [tɕi˥], Cantonese gai1, and the transmitted Shuowen/Guangyun entries. It lists oracle forms, late Shang bronze examples, Chu slips, Shuowen forms, and Qin slips as separate script witnesses. Its dictionary material cites early classical chicken references including 《詩·鄭風》“女曰鷄鳴”; these establish early literary use but do not by themselves date the graph’s semantic development. It also records later senses and compounds such as insect names, fungi, and plants; these are lexical extensions or compounds, not evidence for the graph’s original formation.
evidence.title: 鸡 jī - 漢典

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, Taiwan Ministry of Education
evidence.text: The dictionary treats 鷄 as a graphic variant of 雞, citing Shuowen’s statement that it is the Zhou-script form written with 鳥, and records later dictionaries treating 鷄 and 雞 as equivalent in sound and meaning. It also records 鳮 as a variant and cites a cross-strait simplification comparison associating 鷄 with that form. This supports 鳮 as an attested simplified-style variant; the inspected page does not establish that modern simplified 鸡 arose by a single direct historical replacement of 奚 with 又.
evidence.title: [A04465-001] 鷄 (雞) - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 中华人民共和国国务院, 《汉字简化方案》 digital transcription at Wikisource
evidence.field: 国务院决议; 汉字简化第二表; 汉字偏旁简化表
evidence.text: The 1956-01-28 resolution says the first table was to be used from 1956-02-01 and lists 230 simplified characters; the second table lists 鳮（雞）. The component table lists 鸟（鳥）. This documents the officially published simplified spelling’s relation to 鳮 and the simplified bird component. It does not independently explain the pre-1956 history of 鳮, nor warrant saying that 鸡 formed historically as a semantic compound 又 + 鸟.
evidence.title: 汉字简化方案

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The database reports a Mawangdui silk manuscript use of 雞通假為谿, meaning valley/stream; it contrasts the A copy’s 溪. This is a whole-graph phonetic loan in that textual use, distinct from 奚’s role as a sound element inside the compound 雞. The page does not supply the phonetic values at the time of borrowing or establish the direction and precise date of the loan beyond the manuscript witness.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

evidence.text: The database analyzes oracle forms as pictures of a chicken emphasizing comb and open beak; it says 奚 was later added as a phonetic marker when the picture could be confused with other birds. It reports an oracle-bone use as a place name in 《合集》37363; Qin slips use 雞 for chicken, including the Shuihudi annals entry dated by the text as 十二月甲午; and a Mawangdui 《老子乙本》 line 65 use 雞 for 谿 “valley/stream,” with 溪 in the A copy and 谿 in the Fu Yi text.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

evidence.field: 《說文》; 字形分析; 音韻資料
evidence.text: The database quotes the Shuowen account 雞，知時畜也。从隹，奚聲。鷄，籀文雞，从鳥. It reports that Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin forms and later use 隹, citing Ji Xusheng. Thus the graphic history is not simply 隹 throughout, nor is 鳥 only a modern substitute.

These details concern 奚 as an independent graph and do not give it a semantic role in 雞.

This supports a variant relationship, not necessarily a linear derivation from one shape to the other.

These readings are character readings; they do not independently establish the historical name or sound of a depicted chicken in any borrowing theory.

evidence.field: Mandarin and Old Chinese reading table
evidence.text: This secondary reference lists modern Beijing pinyin jī, Middle Chinese Baxter transcription kej, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤe for 雞; it separately lists Zhengzhang *keː. The two Old Chinese reconstructions belong to distinct systems and should not be combined. The локal TSV cross-check described in the dossier gives the same 雞 Baxter–Sagart form but no externally verified exact upstream row was found in this run.
evidence.title: 雞 - Wiktionary

evidence.field: Mandarin and Old Chinese reading table
evidence.text: The inspected entry supplies Mandarin xī for 奚 and separate historical systems. The search/opened material did not verify the exact Baxter–Sagart row upstream; the repository TSV noted in the dossier records *[g]ˤe, while the secondary material surfaced in search appeared to give other-system forms. Therefore exact system-specific correspondence should be stated cautiously; the independent support for 奚’s phonetic role here is Shuowen’s explicit “奚聲,” not a claim of identical Old Chinese reconstructions.
evidence.title: 奚 - 维基词典

evidence.text: The page identifies 雞-oracle.svg as a digital vector image representing an oracle-script form, lists the Sinica database and other character references as sources, and states that the SVG representation is released to the public domain. This is a modern redraw, not a photograph or rubbing of an inscribed oracle bone.
evidence.title: File:雞-oracle.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.text: The same file page lists a linked “Shuowen seal” version as another script depiction. The available page describes this as a digitally created SVG of a historical script form, not an ancient artifact image, and grants public-domain reuse for the SVG representation.
evidence.title: File:雞-oracle.svg - Wikimedia Commons

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

search_audit.query: 雞 雞字源 上古音 奚 Baxter Sagart kˤe [g]ˤe; 雞 jī modern Mandarin pronunciation 奚 xī pronunciation dictionary official
search_audit.outcome: Opened CUHK pages and found secondary phonological tables. Mandarin and transmitted Middle Chinese information surfaced; exact upstream Baxter–Sagart rows for both 雞 and 奚 were not verifiable from the official dataset publisher during this run.

gaps: The inspected paleographic database summarizes forms but does not expose legible glyph images in the text view; no glyph was visually inspected here.

The sources differ or vary by period on whether the bird semantic element is written 鳥 or 隹: Shuowen calls 鷄 a Zhou-script form from 鳥, CUHK reports Qi/Chu forms from 鳥 and Qin onward from 隹, and the Sinica page summarizes a transition to 隹 + 奚. Exact sequence and dating remain incompletely established by the inspected pages.

A sound component’s pronunciation has been compared in local Baxter–Sagart rows, but an official upstream page verifying those exact TSV rows was not inspected. Thus the local reconstructions remain a cross-check, not external evidence; the source citation URL is only the publisher’s general site.

Modern readings verified here include Mandarin jī and Cantonese gai1. The input’s Japanese and Korean readings were not researched in external sources because they are not needed to establish the Chinese graphic history.
The Mawangdui 雞 ~ 谿 loan report lacks sound values and a demonstrated borrowing rationale in the inspected source; semantic detail and exact phonological motivation remain unresolved.
The exact graphic route from older 鳮 to standardized 鸡 is not fully documented by the inspected official resolution. Treating 鸡 as a semantic compound 又 + 鸟 is unsupported by the inspected evidence.

No proposed borrowing of the spoken word “chicken” from an animal/tool name is needed or supported here. The possible wider areal comparisons listed in the imported dossier were not independently investigated in this research pass.

The CUHK account places a chicken-like pictogram in oracle script, but its first use as a place name does not by itself establish that the earliest semantic value was the animal; no securely dated ordinary chicken-use attestation was independently checked before the reported Qin slips.

The cited Qin slip and Mawangdui text are reported by CUHK; exact archaeological/manuscript dating was not separately verified in this run. The Mawangdui 雞~谿 whole-graph loan report gives no contemporary pronunciations or demonstrated phonological motive. It is distinct from 奚’s phonetic-component role.

There is no independent requirement or evidence here for borrowing the spoken word for chicken from the name of a depicted tool/object; no such etymology is proposed. The chicken pictogram’s exact earliest referent and chronology are not fully established by the pages inspected.

The actual queried Xiaoxuetang page did not expose character-specific glyph records or direct image URLs in the browser output, so no Xiaoxuetang candidate could be selected. The CC0 policy was inspected, but it cannot establish the rights of images from other Sinica databases.

Commons direct SVG URL access yielded a cache miss in the web tool; the file description page itself was accessible and supplies the direct original-file link and public-domain assertion. The proposed file is a modern redraw, not an artifact photograph.

Local Baxter–Sagart TSV exact rows could not be independently verified at an official upstream HTTP page in this turn. Treat local notation as an unverified structured-data cross-check, not external evidence; do not silently reconcile it with Zhengzhang or other reconstruction systems.

The inspected standardized scheme transcription’s second table shows 鳮（雞）, but the exact route from 鳮 through graphic simplification to modern 鸡 is not fully established. The modern form should not be analyzed as a historical 又 + 鸟 compound.

Wiktionary was used only for separate-system phonological comparison; it is secondary and cannot resolve differences between reconstruction systems or establish early semantic chronology. No later semantic extensions were dated in the primary sources inspected.

items.period: Oracle-bone script tradition; approximate late Shang attribution in the file naming/project, not an individually dated artifact
items.caption: This modern redraw presents an oracle-script form interpreted as a chicken pictograph, with a prominent head and crest. The form’s first reported use is as a place name, so its earliest referent is not certain.
items.alt: Black oracle-script character with a large oval head, crest-like strokes, and an elongated body with trailing strokes.
items.selection_reason: Visually legible and relevant to the proposed pictographic origin of 雞; the account associates early oracle forms with a chicken picture, while noting that the reported oracle use is a place name.
items.rights: Public domain dedication for this modern SVG redraw, as stated on the Commons file page.

limitations.text: The image is a modern vector redraw, not an ancient inscription. The depicted form supports a pictographic interpretation, but the earliest use reported for the graph is as a place name and does not establish its original referent with certainty.

The two supplied candidates show identical pixels, and the second candidate is not a distinct seal-script glyph. The evidence identifies the Commons page as a modern redraw and only notes a linked seal-script version; it does not provide a separate image for that form.
